result: High-frequency optogenetic activation of layer II/III pyramidal cells induces frequency-dependent vasoconstriction in cortical slices. Photostimulation at 1-5 Hz failed to elicit reliable vascular responses, while 10 Hz induced vasoconstriction in 4 of 5 arterioles (AUC = -1.7 ± 1.1 x 10³ %.s), and 20 Hz induced vasoconstriction in all arterioles (AUC = -3.7 ± 0.7 x 10³ %.s, n=10). The vasoconstriction magnitude at 20 Hz was statistically different from lower frequencies (p<0.05 vs 1, 2, and 5 Hz).
evaluation: Claims C6-C69 and C76 provide converging evidence from electrophysiological recordings (C52-C56), vascular imaging (C57-C66), and statistical analyses (C67-C69) demonstrating frequency-dependent vasoconstriction. The data show clear dose-response relationships with appropriate controls (wild-type mice, C75) and exclusion of confounds (cortical spreading depression, C70-C73). Sample sizes are adequate (n=4-10 arterioles per condition) with statistical significance reported.

result: Optogenetic stimulation induces a frequency-dependent increase in pyramidal cell somatic Ca²⁺ that precedes vasoconstriction. The Ca²⁺ response at 20 Hz (ΔF/F0 = 79.5 ± 17.7%, n=9 cells) was more than twice that at 2 Hz (ΔF/F0 = 34.5 ± 3.7%, n=9 cells; p=0.024), while the number of evoked spikes was approximately five times higher.
evaluation: Claims C79-C84 demonstrate a clear correlation between stimulation frequency, Ca²⁺ elevation, and spike number using combined electrophysiology and calcium imaging (Figure 2). The statistical comparison is appropriate (t-test, p=0.024), and the temporal relationship (Ca²⁺ increase precedes vasoconstriction) is established. However, the claim that Ca²⁺ increase "precedes" vasoconstriction could be more rigorously demonstrated with simultaneous measurements.

result: Pyramidal cell-induced vasoconstriction requires action potential firing and partially involves glutamatergic transmission. TTX (1 µM) completely abolished vasoconstriction (AUC = 0.4 ± 0.4 x 10³ %.s, n=6, p<0.001), while glutamate receptor antagonists reduced vasoconstriction magnitude by approximately half (AUC = -1.6 ± 0.4 x 10³ %.s, p=0.016).
evaluation: Claims C86-C94 provide strong pharmacological evidence with appropriate controls. TTX experiments (C86-C88) definitively establish AP-dependence, while glutamate receptor antagonist experiments (C92-C93) demonstrate partial involvement. The ~50% reduction with glutamate antagonists suggests additional mechanisms, which is appropriately acknowledged (C94). Statistical tests are appropriate with significant p-values.

result: Prostaglandins derived mainly from COX-2 activity mediate pyramidal cell-induced vasoconstriction both ex vivo and in vivo. Ex vivo, indomethacin (5 µM) completely abolished vasoconstriction (AUC = 0.0 ± 0.2 x 10³ %.s, n=10, p<0.001). In vivo, indomethacin reversed the constriction phase (AUCCtrl = -291.5 ± 92.4 %.s vs AUCIndo = 332.4 ± 184.4 %.s, p=0.016). COX-2 inhibitor NS-398 was more potent than COX-1 inhibitor SC-560.
evaluation: Claims C115-C125 provide robust evidence across both ex vivo and in vivo preparations with appropriate pharmacological controls. The complete abolition by indomethacin and NS-398, combined with partial reduction by SC-560, supports the predominant role of COX-2. The in vivo validation (C117-C120) strengthens the ex vivo findings. Statistical analyses are appropriate with significant p-values. Sample sizes are adequate (n=7-10).

result: PGE2-induced vasoconstriction primarily acts through EP1 receptors and, to a lesser extent, EP3 receptors. EP1 antagonist ONO-8130 reduced vasoconstriction (AUC = 0.3 ± 0.3 x 10³ %.s, p<0.001), while EP3 antagonist L-798,106 had a lesser effect (AUC = -0.9 ± 0.4 x 10³ %.s, p<0.001). Exogenous PGE2 induced dose-dependent vasoconstriction that persisted after removal and was independent of AP firing.
evaluation: Claims C126-C140 provide comprehensive pharmacological evidence for PGE2 receptor involvement. The differential effects of EP1 vs EP3 antagonists are well-documented with appropriate statistics. Exogenous PGE2 experiments (C136-C138) support direct vascular effects. The FP receptor antagonist AL-8810 showed a trend but did not reach significance (C130-C131, p=0.053), which is appropriately reported. The claim about AP-independence (C140) is supported by TTX experiments with exogenous PGE2.

result: Subpopulations of layer II-III pyramidal cells express the molecular machinery for cell-autonomous PGE2 and PGF2α synthesis. Single-cell RT-PCR revealed that COX-1 (25%, n=4/16) and COX-2 (31%, n=5/16) were never co-expressed. Most cells expressed cPGES (88%, n=14/16), and all COX-2 positive neurons co-expressed both PGES and PGFS. Approximately half of pyramidal cells express all transcripts necessary for PGE2 and PGF2α synthesis.
evaluation: Claims C98-C114 provide detailed molecular characterization using single-cell RT-PCR (n=16 cells). The mutually exclusive expression of COX-1 and COX-2 (C100) is clearly demonstrated. The high detection rate of PGES enzymes and systematic co-expression patterns support the conclusion about cell-autonomous synthesis capacity. However, the sample size (n=16) is modest, and protein-level validation would strengthen these mRNA-based findings.

result: Neurogenic vasoconstriction involves NPY-releasing interneurons acting on Y1 receptors and astrocytes via 20-HETE, but not via K+ release through BK channels. Y1 receptor antagonist BIBP3226 abolished vasoconstriction (AUC = -0.3 ± 0.2 x 10³ %.s, p<0.001), while CYP450 ω-hydroxylase inhibitor HET-0016 reduced it (AUC = -1.6 ± 0.7 x 10³ %.s, p=0.016). BK channel blocker paxilline had no effect (AUC = -3.7 ± 0.3 x 10³ %.s, p=1).
evaluation: Claims C143-C151 provide clear pharmacological evidence for intermediary cell involvement. The complete abolition by BIBP3226 (C148-C149) demonstrates critical NPY/Y1 involvement, while partial reduction by HET-0016 (C145-C146) supports astrocytic 20-HETE contribution. The lack of effect with paxilline (C143-C144) appropriately rules out BK channel involvement. Statistical analyses are sound with adequate sample sizes (n=10 per condition).

result: The Emx1-cre;Ai32 transgenic mouse model expresses ChR2H134R in cortical glutamatergic neurons, conferring robust pyramidal cell photoexcitability. Control experiments in wild-type mice lacking ChR2 showed no vascular response to 20 Hz photostimulation.
evaluation: Claims C50-C51 and C75 establish the validity of the optogenetic model with appropriate citations and negative controls. The wild-type control (C75) rules out light-induced artifacts. However, the manuscript could benefit from quantification of ChR2 expression levels and spatial distribution beyond the qualitative description.

result: The observed vasoconstriction is not due to cortical spreading depression. The rate of change in light transmittance associated with cell swelling remained below the threshold for cortical spreading depression (all <2 %.s⁻¹).
evaluation: Claims C70-C73 appropriately address a potential confound. The quantitative criterion (dΔT/dt <2 %.s⁻¹) based on Zhou et al., 2010 is clearly stated and data are provided in Table 1. This control strengthens the interpretation that vasoconstriction is a direct consequence of pyramidal cell activity rather than spreading depression.

result: Background claims establish that neurovascular coupling links neuronal activity to cerebral blood flow and is essential for brain function. While vasodilation mechanisms are well-documented, vasoconstriction mechanisms remain less understood.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 and C13-C18 provide appropriate context from established literature with proper citations. These background claims accurately characterize the state of the field and motivate the study's focus on vasoconstriction mechanisms. The citations are appropriate and support the statements made.

result: Prior work demonstrates that the correlation between neuronal activity and cerebral blood flow is not always maintained, including cases where vasodilation occurs without substantial neuronal response, neuronal activity occurs without increased hemodynamics, and pathological conditions show vasoconstriction with intense activity.
evaluation: Claims C19-C23 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims establish the complexity of neurovascular coupling and provide context for the current findings. The citations support the statements, though the authors should verify that they accurately represent the cited work.

result: Methodological considerations establish that ex vivo brain slices provide controlled environments for pharmacological studies but lack connectivity and blood flow, requiring in vivo validation. Chronic anesthetized animals provide a valuable model for validation despite reduced network activity.
evaluation: Claims C29-C37 appropriately discuss the strengths and limitations of different experimental approaches. The acknowledgment of ex vivo limitations (C30-C31) and the rationale for using anesthetized animals for validation (C35-C37) demonstrate methodological rigor. The citation to Rungta et al., 2021 supports the claim about slowed but preserved NVC in anesthetized animals.

result: Prior work has identified multiple vasodilatory messengers but fewer vasoconstrictor mechanisms. GABAergic interneurons releasing NPY and astrocytes via 20-HETE or K+ are known vasoconstrictors, but pyramidal cell involvement has been overlooked.
evaluation: Claims C38-C43 accurately characterize prior knowledge with appropriate citations. The statement that pyramidal cell involvement has been overlooked (C43) is supported by the literature review and motivates the current study. However, the authors should verify that no prior studies have examined pyramidal cell-mediated vasoconstriction.

result: PGE2 is a bimodal messenger that can induce either vasodilation or vasoconstriction depending on concentration and site of action. Under physiological conditions, PGE2 is produced by astrocytes (via COX-1) or pyramidal cells (via COX-2). The hypothesis is proposed that pyramidal cells may be responsible for vasoconstriction when spiking activity is high.
evaluation: Claims C44-C49 provide appropriate background with citations supporting the bimodal nature of PGE2 and its cellular sources. The hypothesis (C49) is clearly stated as speculation based on prior work. This sets up the experimental investigation that follows. The citations appropriately support the background claims.

result: Background on vasoactive substance release establishes that vasodilatory substance synthesis/release requires intracellular Ca²⁺ elevation, but little is known about vasoconstrictor release. Action potentials in pyramidal cells induce both somatic Ca²⁺ elevation and glutamate release.
evaluation: Claims C77-C78 and C85 provide appropriate background with citations (Attwell et al., 2010; Cauli and Hamel, 2010; Smetters et al., 1999). These claims establish the rationale for examining Ca²⁺ dynamics and glutamate involvement. The characterization of the knowledge gap (C78) is appropriate.

result: Potential mechanisms are proposed whereby high glutamate levels from pyramidal cells may activate NPY interneurons or astrocytes through ionotropic/metabotropic receptors, or directly activate NMDA receptors on smooth muscle cells.
evaluation: Claims C90-C91 are speculative hypotheses supported by citations but not directly tested in this study. While the citations support these possibilities, the claims are presented as potential mechanisms rather than demonstrated findings. The subsequent experiments (C92-C93) show glutamate involvement but don't definitively establish which of these mechanisms operates.

result: PGE2 released by pyramidal cells can activate astrocytes and neurons, which express PGE2 receptors.
evaluation: Claims C141-C142 are supported by appropriate citations (Clasadonte et al., 2011; Di Cesare et al., 2006; Tasic et al., 2016; Zeisel et al., 2015). These claims provide context for the indirect mechanisms examined in the study. The citations appropriately support the receptor expression patterns.

result: Summary conclusions establish that pyramidal cell activity leads to arteriolar vasoconstriction in a frequency-dependent manner correlating with Ca²⁺ increase. The response involves PGE2 from COX-2 pyramidal cells acting on EP1/EP3 receptors, with intermediary roles for NPY interneurons and astrocytes via 20-HETE.
evaluation: Claims C152-C158 appropriately summarize the major findings supported by the experimental data. These conclusions are well-supported by the grouped results above. The summary accurately reflects the relative contributions of different mechanisms (PGE2 as primary, NPY and 20-HETE as intermediary).
